The proposed answer of 6836 is incorrect. I get **6992**.

**Setup.** The lattice has 61 points. Removing the center leaves 60 points, arranged in 6 sectors of 10 points each. A triangle strictly contains O exactly when its vertices (other than O) have three distinct directions from O and no closed half-plane through O contains all three. This also rules out degenerate triangles.

**Directions.** Each sector (angles 60k to 60k+60) has directions at offsets 0°, 13.9°, 19.1°, 30°, 40.9°, 46.1°, with multiplicities 4, 1, 1, 2, 1, 1. Across the 36 directions, six have multiplicity 4, six have multiplicity 2, and twenty-four have multiplicity 1. The multiplicities sum to 60.

**Triples with three distinct directions.** Let p₁ = 60, p₂ = Σm² = 144, p₃ = Σm³ = 456. Then
e₃ = (p₁³ − 3p₁p₂ + 2p₃)/6 = (216000 − 25920 + 912)/6 = 31832.
(Check: C(60,3) = 34220, and triples with a repeated direction number 2388, giving 34220 − 2388 = 31832.)

**Bad triples.** With distinct directions, at most one angular gap is ≥ 180°. Assign each bad triple to the point A that follows that large gap. The other two points must lie in the half-open arc (θ_A, θ_A + 180°].
- For every direction, this arc contains exactly 30 points. This holds because the arc consists of the later offsets in the same sector, two full sectors, and the earlier offsets in the opposite sector, and the sector totals always sum to 30.
- The sum of C(m,2) over the arc is always 21, since the full set of same-direction pairs totals 42 and the arc contains exactly half.
- So each point A gives C(30,2) − 21 = 435 − 21 = 414 bad pairs.
- Total bad triples: 60 × 414 = 24840.

**Good triples.** 31832 − 24840 = **6992**.

As a check on the method, I verified it on small configurations: four axis points give 0 good triples, and three points at 0°, 120°, 240° give 1.

The proposed value 6836 does not match this count of 6992.

VERDICT: REJECT
